answer: The question's premise is not something I can verify from a specific source, so this is a reasoned explanation rather than a confirmed finding. DeepWalk trains skip-gram with stochastic gradient descent on node sequences from truncated random walks, so each node is paired with many neighbors up to several hops away within a context window. LINE(2nd) instead samples direct edges and uses second-order proximity with negative sampling, so it sees only one-hop neighborhoods per update. On a sparse citation graph like DBLP PaperCitation, where many nodes have few direct links, the multi-hop co-occurrences from walks give more training signal per node and capture community structure more robustly. The SGD scheme with repeated walks and a decaying learning rate therefore tends to yield better-generalizing embeddings, though the exact reason in the source paper may differ.
